articles.title: The midterms are going to be a data security nightmare
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s efforts to obtain state voter lists in a stated effort to prevent fraud are more likely to disenfranchise legit voters, experts say.
articles.body: One messy database is threatening to disenfranchise thousands or even millions of registered voters, while leaving even more at risk of intimidation or data breaches, in the name of solving a problem that barely exists. As the 2026 midterm elections approach, election and privacy experts are sounding alarms about the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) Program, which President Donald Trump’s administration has expanded to ostensibly catch noncitizens voting. Experts say that amounts to a dangerous, error-prone effort to centralize voter data. “The federal government doesn’t have the authority to do any of that and doesn’t have the expertise either,” says Eileen O’Connor, senior counsel at the Brennan Center. “Inserting themselves into the day-to-day functioning of state elections is unprecedented and disturbing.” The SAVE program, created in 1987 to verify public benefit eligibility, queries federal databases to determine residents’ immigration status. Last year, Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) began demanding nearly every state provide complete voter information to cross-reference against the program, then purge any voters the agency deems ineligible within 45 days. These state rolls can include reams of sensitive information, including social security numbers, driver’s license numbers, and in some cases, voter participation history. Zach Kahler, a spokesperson for US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the part of DHS that administers the SAVE program, said the administration “is dedicated to securing America’s elections,” and called it “critical that states have the information needed to administer fair and secure elections.” DOJ spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told The Verge that the agency has authority under laws like the National Voter Registration Act to “ensure that states have proper voter registration procedures and programs to maintain clean voter rolls containing only eligible voters in federal elections.” Those challenging it say the agency is going far beyond its authority. But while some states have successfully fought the order, 16 have agreed to hand over full voter registration lists, according to the Brennan Center, and two — Texas and Alaska — agreed to implement the purge. In October of 2025, Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson said an audit of over 18 million against SAVE data had identified 2,724 registered “potential noncitizens.” The state told local counties to further investigate the discrepancies and refer those they confirmed to be noncitizens to the state attorney general. But SAVE is an unreliable indicator of citizenship. Among other places, it pulls from the Social Security Administration (SSA), which acknowledges that its information is only a “snapshot in time,” that can give “an indication of citizenship,” rather than “definitive information.” Recently naturalized citizens — who can legally draw benefits or register to vote — may not be recognized by this snapshot. DHS itself acknowledges that users of the program must verify any output besides “United States Citizen.” Multiple studies as well as state investigations have found that extraordinarily few noncitizens vote in US elections. A 2014 analysis published in The Washington Post, for example, found 31 credible instances of voter impersonation out of a billion cast ballots since 2000. Nelson claims that “The Trump Administration’s decision to give states free and direct access to this data set for the first time has been a game changer,” but many elections and privacy experts say that’s not a good thing. States have always been in charge of administering elections, and have the processes in place to do so. Demands for unredacted voter files only exert undue control over elections and subject voters to increased privacy risks, they say. “The administration has proceeded in the face of that known risk, some might say by design, rather than just out of negligence,” says John Davisson, deputy director and director of enforcement at the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), which has sued to block the expansion of SAVE. “And it’s resulting in people losing the right to vote.” The risk is not hypothetical. Outlets including NPR and The Texas Tribune have identified US citizens erroneously flagged via SAVE. “If people feel that they’re going to be potentially subject to prosecution and investigation, despite the fact that they’re legally entitled to vote, it will tend to drive down registration rates,” Davisson says. “It will tend to create a culture of fear that limits democratic participation.” It’s also part of a larger pattern of potential intimidation: Trump has floated sending Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or the National Guard to polling stations to ensure “honest elections,” even though armed federal agents are generally barred from deploying there. O’Connor, who previously worked at the voting section of the DOJ Civil Rights Division, says the agency would rarely ask states to produce complete voter rolls before Trump. When they did, it was typically for a court case or specific investigation. “This is just a vacuuming effort,” she says. This is just the latest Trump administration effort to centralize agency data. The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), for example, attempted to build a massive database combining information on individuals across multiple agencies, eschewing typical data security protections, The Washington Post reported. While you might think that the government already has tons of information on you, there’s still plenty of data that only states maintain, like driver’s license numbers and voting history. The Census Bureau goes to great lengths to assure residents that it protects their privacy, because failing to do so could jeopardize the entire project of counting up the population (Trump has arguably compromised this, pushing to change the Census to identify and exclude undocumented immigrants). The Privacy Act of 1974 also limits how federal agencies can share information with one another. Amassing voter information, O’Connor says, is a way some Republicans “are now laying the groundwork to be able to call into question the results of future elections, should they not go the way that they want them to go.” Recently a Florida US Attorney’s Office brought on Kurt Olsen, a 2020 election denier, as a senior attorney. Large collections of personal information can also be attractive targets for hackers. The infamous 2015 breach of the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) exposed sensitive information on over 22 million people, including federal employees, contractors, and their friends and families, which is partly why experts were concerned about DOGE’s data consolidation efforts. EPIC found the DOJ’s promised safeguards for voter rolls are “littered with ambiguous security promises and empty recitations.” The Trump administration likely won’t be able to actually create the unified voting list of its dreams, but it could still have costs. Davisson points to President Donald Trump’s recent executive order demanding the Postal Service withhold mail-in ballots to homes unless states submit their voter rolls to the feds. “They’re trying to prevent those people from being able to vote by mail, which is a critical means of exercising the right to vote in this day and age,” he says. “And they’re doing that through the exploitation of personal information through the creation of these lists.” State and local officials are supposed to have final say over their voter rolls, and citizens may get the chance to correct the record — Davisson suggests checking in advance with local election officials. But they could also easily miss a notice and be disenfranchised, or fear they’ll get in trouble for pushing back. “The system should be working to ensure their fundamental right to vote,” Davisson says. “So it is disgraceful that this is a problem that individuals have to worry about now.” Update, June 18th: Added comment from USCIS.

articles.title: President Donald Trump Claims, "Tariffs Are Making Us Much Richer," but Economists Show They Have Unintended Consequences
articles.summary: The costs of tariffs to consumers, the U.S. economy, and the stock market may be considerably greater than the revenue they bring in over the next decade.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has been in the White House for nearly six years, spanning two nonconsecutive terms. Over that time, the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and growth-dependent Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have delivered well-above-average annual returns, compared to most other presidents since the late 1890s.

One of the key catalysts powering Wall Street's bull market, the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, was well underway before Trump's second term began. But make no mistake about it: Wall Street and investors have also benefited immensely from the president's Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (signed into law in December 2017), which lowered the peak marginal corporate income tax rate to 21% (the lowest rate since 1939), fueling record S&P 500 share buybacks.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

President Trump's tariff and trade policy may be doing more harm than good. Image source: Official White House Photo by Molly Riley.

Tariffs are my favorite word. They're going to make America rich. It's making us much richer than we ever thought. We're taking in trillions of dollars.

While the projection for tariff revenue has, indeed, soared over the next decade, Trump's tariffs also come with an assortment of unintended consequences, according to economists.

President Trump is leaning heavily on tariffs

Although we've been hearing a lot about tariffs during Trump's second term, they've been a theme throughout his presidency. In 2018, the president imposed tariffs on an assortment of goods from China, sparking a trade war.

In early April 2025, Donald Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" tariffs, consisting of a sweeping global duty and higher reciprocal tariffs on dozens of countries deemed to have unfavorable trade imbalances with America. These tariffs remained in place until the U.S. Supreme Court struck them down in a February 2026 ruling.

articles.title: Jamie Dimon warns US savers about Washington’s ‘heroin’ effect — it could crush you. Here’s how his bank protects itself
articles.summary: Hint: It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Washington has a way of making the economy feel good. But Jamie Dimon wants Americans to look at what's fueling the high.

Speaking at the Economic Club of Chicago earlier this month, the CEO of JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) compared government spending to a powerful drug — one that can boost corporate profits while setting the stage for a painful aftermath.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

"We've got to remember about government spending: It's inflationary," he said (1). "It also does something which is unbelievable — makes you all feel good. It's like heroin. It drives your corporate profits."

For Americans watching their savings, that's a troubling combination. Businesses can report stronger earnings while the dollars you've worked to put away buy less at the grocery store, gas station and checkout counter.

Dimon explained how the money moves through the economy: "When governments spend a trillion dollars, that goes into spending, that goes into all your businesses. Machine tools, burgers, pools, homes."

"And then we all feel good because we're all making a lot of money," he said. "And it's a little bit of a false thing if it's inflationary, which it is."

Washington's borrowing habit gives that warning plenty of weight.

According to Treasury Department data (2), the U.S. government spent $7.40 trillion in fiscal 2026 while collecting $5.40 trillion in revenue, resulting in a deficit of $1.99 trillion — an increase of $217 billion from fiscal 2025.

Dimon made clear that his concern stretches beyond one administration's signature legislation.

"It wasn't the One Big Beautiful Bill, guys," he said. "We have been profligate now for years."

So how does America's biggest bank protect itself?

It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.

"We prepare for low rates, high rates, stock price down 40%, credit spreads going up, bond rates at 8%, high yield at 15%," Dimon said. "And JPMorgan can handle all of that."

For everyday Americans, the inflationary pain Dimon warned about is already hitting home. U.S. consumer prices have climbed 29.8% (3) since the beginning of 2020, with energy prices soaring 53.5% (4) over the same period.

articles.title: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.summary: Account takeover threats go beyond stolen passwords as criminals exploit session cookies, SIM swaps and MFA fatigue to bypass your login security.
articles.body: You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device. Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself. Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES 1. Stolen login sessions When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step. How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session. 2. SIM swaps and phone account fraud Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password-reset message you did not request. How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone. ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU? 3. Fake login approvals and MFA fatigue Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code. How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals. 4. Malware and risky browser extensions An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual. How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure. 5. Malicious apps with access to your accounts Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password. This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions. How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features. Passkeys can help, but they are not the whole answer Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process. How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current. If a service offers backup recovery codes, store them securely so you can regain access if your primary device is lost or damaged. Why changing your password may not be enough Changing a compromised password is important, but it may not automatically remove every form of unauthorized access. Some services revoke existing sessions after a password change, while others require you to sign out of devices separately. A criminal might also have established another route into your account, such as an app-specific password, an unauthorized connected application or a new recovery method. Your email deserves particular attention. Someone with access to your inbox could create forwarding rules that quietly send copies of your messages elsewhere. Review security settings for unfamiliar recovery addresses, connected devices, forwarding rules and app permissions. Remove anything you did not authorize. Also, check whether your password was reused elsewhere. If it was, replace those passwords with unique credentials. A password manager can make this easier without requiring you to memorize every login. What to do if someone gets around your password If you suspect an account takeover, act quickly. Start with the account that controls access to your other accounts, usually your primary email. Here's where to focus: A credit freeze is free and can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. You must contact all three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, to freeze your reports at each bureau. If you believe someone has stolen your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan from the Federal Trade Commission. The value of watching beyond the login Strong account security is essential, but identity misuse can happen outside the original account. A criminal might use exposed personal information to apply for credit, take over a mobile account or attempt financial fraud without triggering a traditional password alert. That's where an identity theft protection service can provide another layer of monitoring. These services can monitor certain financial accounts, credit activity and exposed personal information for signs of suspicious activity. Some also provide identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if your identity is stolen. Features vary by provider and plan, and no service can prevent every form of identity theft. For additional peace of mind, consider a service that offers monitoring, timely alerts and recovery assistance. See my picks for the best identity theft protection services at Cyberguy.com to compare your options and find the right coverage for your needs. Pro tip: Protect the accounts that unlock everything else Once a month, review active sessions for your main email and financial accounts. Remove devices you no longer use and check whether your recovery information or connected app permissions have changed. Pay attention to unexpected login alerts, changes to your mobile account and new financial activity. A short monthly security check can help you spot suspicious changes before they become a larger problem. FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER Kurt's key takeaways For years, I've told people to use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. I still stand by that advice. But what concerns me now is how criminals can get into accounts without ever knowing the password. Think about someone quietly reading your email through a connected app you forgot about or using a stolen login session to access information you've worked hard to protect. You might change your password and assume everything is fine, while that access remains open. That's why I recommend checking which devices and apps have access to your most important accounts. Start with email and your mobile carrier, because losing control of either can create problems with your financial accounts. And while identity theft monitoring services can help alert you to certain suspicious activity, they work best alongside strong account security. A few minutes reviewing your settings today could save you a great deal of trouble later. Have you ever received a login approval or password-reset request you didn't initiate, and did you take action or ignore it? articles.title: Binance recovers 90 percent of stolen assets from hack
articles.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform. On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection…
articles.body:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform.

On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection with the incident.

“All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%,” the company said in post on social platform X on Saturday. “We will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and OTC channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.”

The company also said it will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not the users. In a previous update , Binance said it had set aside $6.34B in company funds to cover hacked losses.

President Trump said Friday that the administration is looking into the incident. When asked if the hack should be attributed to a suspected North Korean hacker group, the president said, “we don’t know.”

According to two blockchain intelligence firms, TRM Labs and Chainalysis, a North Korea-based cybercrime group TraderTraitor appeared to be behind the hacking incident. TRM Labs also noted that several aspects of the latest hack matched earlier North Korea-linked incidents like the $1.5 billion hack of crypto exchange Bybit last year.

In its Saturday update, Binance said after the 90 percent replenishment, the remaining 10 percent consists of “assets are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.”

The company said the replenishment came from a partial deployment of the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund and as well as Binance’s corporate treasury.

articles.title: 'Ferem diretamente o Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina', diz CRM do Paraná sobre alunos que atacaram bolsistas e fizeram alusão ao nazismo | G1
articles.standfirst: Alunos denunciaram as ofensas ao Ministério Público Federal, que apura as mensagens enviadas após o resultado do 2º turno das eleições. UniCesumar afirmou que alunos envolvidos foram expulsos, suspensos ou advertidos "de acordo com a gravidade das condutas".
articles.summary: Alunos denunciaram as ofensas ao Ministério Público Federal, que apura as mensagens enviadas após o resultado do 2º turno das eleições.
articles.body:
Depois da divulgação de mensagens com ataques a bolsistas e referências ao nazismo em um grupo de alunos de uma turma de Medicina de uma faculdade particular de Maringá , no Norte do Paraná, o Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informou que vai acompanhar o caso e "adotará todas as providências cabíveis".

Segundo o CRM, as atitudes dos estudantes ferem os princípios do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, "segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza", diz a nota da instituição.

As mensagens foram enviadas depois do resultado das Eleições de 2026 , em que Lula foi reeleito presidente do Brasil .

Mensagens foram enviadas em um grupo com estudantes de medicina — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A UniCesumar, instituição em que os alunos estudam, destacou que as trocas de mensagens não aconteceram nos canais oficiais da universidade e que adotou medidas disciplinares para punir os alunos envolvidos , incluindo expulsões, suspensões e advertências, "de acordo com a gravidade das condutas".

Alunos de Medicina foram expulsos e suspensos

Neste sábado (31), procurada pelo g1 , a UniCesumar informou que concluiu a sindicância que avaliou o caso e que adotou as medidas disciplinares. A reportagem questionou quantos estudantes receberam cada uma das punições, mas a universidade respondeu que não vai informar.

Em nota, a instituição de ensino também disse repudiar "veementemente qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito".

Alunos da instituição abriram uma denúncia no Ministério Público Federal (MPF) depois dos ataques. O órgão confirmou ter recebido a denúncia sobre as mensagens e disse que apura o caso.

Mensagens fazem ataques a bolsistas e alusão ao nazismo

As mensagens foram enviadas no domingo (25) em um grupo da turma. Em uma delas, um estudante sugere superioridade em relação aos bolsistas ao comparar quem paga a mensalidade com quem conquistou a vaga por seleção acadêmica de programas sociais.

"Quem paga trabalhou e tem 15 mil [reais] por mês para pagar >>>>>>> Quem passou numa provinha", escreveu um outro estudante.

Mensagens foram enviadas em um grupo com estudantes de medicina — Foto: Arquivo

Além disso, imagens e expressões associadas ao nazismo também foram compartilhadas nos grupos. Em uma das mensagens, um estudante compartilhou a foto do exército nazista acompanhada de referências ao "leite cru", expressão que se tornou comum entre grupos na internet que defendem a supremacia branca .

Print da conversa de cunho nazista. — Foto: Reprodução

Outra aluna criticou as ofensas e ressaltou que todos terão a mesma formação, independentemente da forma de ingresso. "Virou bonito ofender quem não tem dinheiro para pagar toda a mensalidade, como vocês? Todo mundo aqui vai sair com CRM [registro profissional para exercer a medicina]", disse.

O g1 optou por não identificar os alunos, uma vez que o caso ainda está sendo investigado pelos órgãos responsáveis e pode envolver menores de idade.

Ao g1, um estudante informou que tanto os universitários que fizeram as ofensas quanto aqueles que foram alvos das mensagens não frequentaram a instituição desde que o caso ganhou repercussão.

"É um clima hostil na faculdade, um clima hostil nos grupos, que vai muito além de divergências políticas. Parece que o contexto da eleição foi apenas um pretexto para eles extravasarem o ódio às pessoas mais pobres", disse o estudante, que preferiu não ser identificado.

Em nota, a UniCesumar afirmou que adotou medidas disciplinares contra os alunos envolvidos nas mensagens, mas não detalhou quantos estudantes foram atingidos pela decisão. Veja a íntegra:

"A UniCesumar comunica que concluiu no dia 30 de outubro a Sindicância Interna aberta para apuração dos fatos envolvendo mensagens trocadas em grupo de WhatsApp por alunos da Instituição.

A Comissão de Sindicância recomendou e a Reitoria da Unicesumar decidiu pela aplicação de medidas disciplinares em relação aos alunos envolvidos, nos termos do Regimento Interno da universidade.

As medidas disciplinares foram: desligamentos do quadro discente da Instituição, advertências e suspensões, de acordo com a gravidade de cada conduta apurada.

A UniCesumar reafirma seu compromisso com a ética, a responsabilidade, o respeito à vida e os valores que orientam a formação de seus estudantes. A Instituição repudia veementemente qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito.

O Núcleo de Apoio ao Estudante de Medicina (NAEME) permanece à disposição dos alunos para oferecer acolhimento, orientação e suporte, nos contatos (44) 99122-3957 ou (44) 3027-6360 ramal 2870.

O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informou que as atitudes descritas ferem os princípios do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina. Confira:

"Tais atitudes ferem diretamente os princípios fundamentais do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza.

A escolha pela Medicina exige compromissos humanísticos e humanitários, pautados pela promoção do bem-estar físico, mental e social dos indivíduos e da coletividade. Atitudes discriminatórias são incompatíveis com esses valores e não devem ser toleradas no ambiente de formação médica.

O CRM-PR adotará todas as providências cabíveis no âmbito de suas atribuições institucionais e acompanhará o desdobramento do caso, contribuindo para que haja uma apuração rigorosa e transparente dos fatos pelas instâncias competentes".

articles.title: Motorista com criança no colo na Ponte Rio-Niterói é flagrado | G1
articles.standfirst: Carro ainda seguia em zigue-zague e quase atingiu motociclistas durante o trajeto.
articles.summary: Motorista com criança no colo na Ponte Rio-Niterói é flagrado em zigue-zague e quase atinge motociclistas; conduta configura infração gravíssima e gera multa.
articles.body:
Um motorista foi flagrado dirigindo com uma criança de menos de 3 anos no colo na Ponte Rio-Niterói neste domingo (1º). O menino por várias vezes colocou a cabeça e parte do corpo para fora da janela e parecia segurar um celular sob o volante .

O carro ainda seguia em zigue-zague e quase atingiu motociclistas durante o trajeto . Ao lado do motorista, era possível ver uma mulher no banco do carona.

As imagens, a que o g1 teve acesso, foram gravadas no início da tarde, no sentido capital da via expressa.

Motorista é flagrado dirigindo com criança no colo na Ponte Rio-Niterói — Foto: Reprodução

Transportar uma criança sem observar as regras específicas de segurança é infração gravíssima , segundo o Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB), e prevê multa de R$ 293,47 e 7 pontos na carteira .

Como o bebê ainda estava no colo do próprio condutor, o caso também pode se enquadrar na proibição de dirigir transportando pessoas entre os braços e as pernas , considerada infração média , de R$ 130,16 e 4 pontos .

A condução em zigue-zague, que colocou motociclistas em risco, também pode caracterizar direção ameaçando outros veículos , outra infração gravíssima .

Segundo as regras do CTB, crianças com menos de 10 anos que ainda não tenham atingido 1,45 metro de altura devem ser transportadas no banco traseiro , com o dispositivo de retenção adequado à idade, ao peso e à altura.

A regulamentação do Conselho Nacional de Trânsito (Contran) estabelece diferentes dispositivos conforme a faixa etária:

Crianças de até 1 ano devem usar o bebê-conforto;

Entre 1 e 4 anos, a regra prevê o uso da cadeirinha;

Ds 4 aos 7 anos e meio, deve ser utilizado o assento de elevação.

Dos 7 anos e meio aos 10 anos, ou enquanto a criança tiver menos de 1,45 metro, o transporte deve ser feito no banco traseiro com cinto de segurança.

O Artigo 168 prevê, além da multa e dos pontos, retenção do veículo até que a situação seja regularizada.

articles.body: Satya Nadella has said that his views on AI have shifted in the past year. The Microsoft CEO was asked what he has changed his mind about in the last 12 months. His answer was about AI alignment, which is how to make sure AI systems do what people intend. Nadella started by looking back to the period around 2018 and 2019. He said that when Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Elon Musk were, as he put it, “one happy family”, they were the real believers in scaling laws. Nadella said that was also what he believed in back then.What has changed Satya Nadella's mind in last 8 yearsNadella said the biggest change in his thinking is on alignment. He used to assume it would take care of itself.“When Dario and Ilya and Sam and Greg and Elon were all, I guess, one happy family, they were really the believers in scaling laws and that’s what I believed in back in 2018 and 2019. And I think the biggest change now I have is: ‘I used to always think that alignment will just fall out. I no longer believe that. So this alignment thing may be a harder, different problem. So that's the one thing I've changed my mind on,” Nadella said during an industry event in Germany recently.Alignment is the practice of designing AI systems so that their goals, behaviour and outputs match human intentions, values and ethical standards.Satya Nadella on companies, governments rushing to patch PHP flawsNadella also reacted to the crisis that unfolded after security firms recorded millions of automated exploitation attempts within hours of a PHP bug’s public disclosure. articles.title: Why daylight saving time ended so early this year
articles.summary: Believe it or not, it’s time again for the twice-a-year clock change.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – They’ve gone and done it again. If you weren’t awake at 2 a.m. Sunday, you missed the clocks “falling back” an hour as daylight saving time came to an end.

Of course, you may have noticed when you woke up and found the clocks in your house that don’t match the time on your phone or laptop. Maybe it was how high in the sky the sun was when you awoke, or how early it seems to set on Sunday night.

You may even catch yourself pondering whether it really is the end of daylight saving time in 2026 already.

It is, but you also aren’t misguided in thinking it feels a little early for the clocks to be falling back.

Daylight saving time always ends on the first Sunday of the month, making November 1 the earliest date that we can set our clocks back an hour. That is what we’re experiencing this year.

Looking ahead, daylight saving time starts on the second Monday of March, meaning the soonest our clocks can “spring forward” is March 8. In 2027, that’s precisely when daylight saving time will start again.

It’s possible, through congressional action, that 2027 will be the last year that the U.S. changes its clocks.

Should the Senate pass the Sunshine Protection Act already passed by the House, and President Trump signs it into law, winters could feel different . Under the legislation, states that do not exempt themselves would observe daylight saving time year-round.

Generally speaking, that also means we would have later sunrises and sunsets than we have experienced between early November and early March. It’s the later sunrises in winter that didn’t sit well with some when the U.S. last observed permanent daylight saving time .

It’s difficult to say when, if ever, the Senate will pick up the Sunshine Protection Act. Many health experts disagree with the legislation , which could also impact how thousands practice their religion and your future flights , at least temporarily. The bill doesn’t have a “clear path forward,” either, according to Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

articles.title: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers
articles.summary: Prop 45 would limit environmental reviews for “essential” infrastructure — one of the biggest controversies is over whether it would carve out loopholes for data centers.
articles.body: A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn. Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law. “The concern here is that data center developers will find a way to shoehorn their projects into the definition of an essential project and then get to take advantage of … the fast-track review that it’ll create,” says Fernando Gaytan, a senior attorney at the nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, which opposes Prop 45. “Communities get cut out of the conversation.” Prop 45 would loosen standards for certain projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). CEQA requires state agencies to perform environmental reviews and work with project developers to find ways to limit any harmful impacts to the environment and public health. Crucially, CEQA also mandates that state agencies gather community input and consider public comment before issuing any approvals. Specifically, Prop 45 would create a 365-day deadline for agencies to complete the environmental impact report for a project. It also stipulates that any legal challenges would need to be settled within 270 days. It would only allow for 45 days of public comment, and it would only require state agencies and developers to consult with Native American tribes that have been federally recognized. CEQA as it’s currently written sets a minimum rather than a maximum number of days for public review, and mandates consultation with tribes that might be impacted by a project even if they’re not formally recognized by the federal government as having “government-to-government” relations with the US. During the CEQA review process, state agencies develop alternatives that developers can take to mitigate environmental and health risks. Prop 45 would turn that on its head, making developers responsible for coming up with a single alternative project plan for regulators to consider. The proposition would also strip away an agency’s authority to repeatedly ask a developer for more information about a proposed project; state regulators would need to specify all the information a company is required to provide at the start of the application process. On top of all that, Prop 45 would bar courts from halting a project altogether even if it finds that the regulatory agency failed to correctly comply with CEQA. The judge would only have the ability to pause specific parts of a project that are problematic, rather than forcing a full stop to construction. That’s the piece that’s most egregious for Gaytan. “It’s hard to undo harms once you’ve already started a project,” he says. Data centers are a hot-button election issue for midterms across the US and have become a point of contention for Prop 45 as well. The proposition lists nine types of “essential” projects that would be eligible for streamlined review, including housing, clean energy, and “broadband Internet access.” Gaytan and some other legal experts contend that the latter designation — broadband internet access — could include data centers. The language includes any project that would “provide mass-market retail service by wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in this state that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service.” Proposed data centers that include any broadband transmission infrastructure might be able to squeeze into that definition, UC Davis School of Law professor emeritus Richard Frank and attorney Matthew McKerley write in a recent column in the Daily Journal. They also point out that companies currently developing data centers have poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into a campaign to support Prop 45. And while Prop 45 excludes certain types of projects, like nuclear energy and dial-up internet access service, it doesn’t explicitly bar data centers. Proponents, meanwhile, argue that Prop 45 would not apply to data centers. “The fact that data centers may play a role in supporting the Internet does not make them ‘essential broadband Internet access projects’ under Prop 45,” attorney and lobbyist Kurt Oneto writes in The National Law Review. The Yes on Prop 45 campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Prop 45 has managed to garner support from the California and Hawaii chapter of the NAACP, which has been among one of the most vocal civil rights organizations to oppose data center developments across the US. The NAACP filed suit against xAI over air pollution from gas turbines at its Colossus 2 data center, and the Texas chapter has called for a statewide moratorium on data center development. “Working families and communities of color pay the highest price when essential projects like housing, clean energy, water, health care facilities, and transportation take years longer and cost millions more than they should,” Rick Callender, president of NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference, said in a September 9th press release. “Prop. 45 is about accountability, not shortcuts, creating a smarter process that gets these projects built sooner while protecting civil rights and environmental safeguards.” Regardless of whether Prop 45 influences data center development in California, its opponents worry that it could disempower the same communities that the new projects it covers are supposed to benefit. “It’s about public participation and democracy,” Gaytan says. “It’s about neighbors being able to say, ‘I want you to be transparent with me about what’s going behind that wall.’”

articles.title: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
articles.summary: The FBI says that malicious actors from North Korea stole $6.3 billion worth of Crypto from Binance customers.
articles.body: The FBI says North Korea was behind the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist that hit Binance on October 29th. The FBI labeled the activity “TraderTraitor” and said that it had observed actors it has connected to hack converting the tokens to Ethereum and preparing for further laundering of the funds. The agency offered few other details or evidence. The statement says: > North Korea Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack > The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor.” > The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages. As expected, Binance reopened customer withdrawals today after freezing them in the immediate aftermath of the hack.

articles.title: Fake party invite scam: Can you trust a friend's reply?
articles.summary: A phishing email disguised as an Evite fooled a man even after he emailed his friend to verify it, revealing how compromised Gmail accounts aid scams.
articles.body: An invitation from a friend lands in your inbox. Something feels off, so you do the responsible thing. You email your friend to make sure the invitation is legitimate. A reply comes back confirming everything. You would probably feel comfortable clicking at that point, right? That's what makes a recent email from John in Westlake, Ohio, so unsettling. He received a suspicious Evite and decided to investigate. However, the response he received raised even more questions. John has since confirmed with his friend that the emails were part of a scam. His experience reveals a potential weakness in how we verify suspicious emails, especially when someone else's inbox may be compromised. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN A suspicious Evite gets an unexpected reply John received what appeared to be a fraudulent Evite from a friend. After reading our previous warnings about fake Evite emails, he decided to email his friend directly rather than click the invitation. What happened next made him even more suspicious. Here's what John wrote: "I received what I thought was a fraudulent eVite from a friend. Thanks to your previous posts, I strongly suspected that this was a phishing attempt. So, I independently emailed my friend and asked if the eVite was legitimate. I got the response below." Hi John This is from me, and I sent it, Sorry for the confusion, Thank you "It appears that the scammers either set up an auto-response on the Gmail account or manually responded to my email. The punctuation was wrong, so I didn't consider the response legitimate." John thought the reply sounded unlike his friend and wondered whether someone had gained access to the account. He later contacted his friend again and confirmed that the emails were a scam. John also shared the actual Evite-branded invitation, which advertised a "Dinner Gathering & Celebration" and included a "View Invitation" button. Its polished design resembled a legitimate event invitation, showing how easily someone could mistake a fraudulent message for the real thing. WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM How a fake party invite scam could manipulate email replies Most people know they should be cautious about unexpected links. In fact, we've repeatedly encouraged readers to verify suspicious messages before taking action. That remains excellent advice. However, there's an additional concern when the email account you're contacting may already be under someone else's control. The Federal Trade Commission warned in May 2026 about fraudulent invitations that imitate popular services such as Evite and Paperless Post. These messages may appear to come from someone you recognize. When you try to view the invitation, a fake website can ask for your email password or a verification code. If criminals obtain access to that account, they may send more fraudulent invitations to the account owner's contacts. The messages can appear to originate from a legitimate email address, making them especially convincing. Now consider what happens when someone replies to one of those invitations asking whether it's real. If a criminal still controls the sender's inbox, that person could potentially intercept the question and send a reassuring answer. A recipient might then believe the invitation is safe because a familiar email address confirmed it. Could scammers set up automatic Gmail replies? John wondered whether someone had configured an automatic response inside his friend's Gmail account. Technically, that's possible. Gmail allows users to create email templates and filters that automatically respond to certain messages. Someone with unauthorized access could potentially misuse that feature or simply respond manually while impersonating the account owner. Although John confirmed the emails were fraudulent, we still don't know how the reassuring reply was generated. There's no technical evidence yet showing whether someone accessed his friend's account, configured an automatic response or used another method to impersonate him. What John's experience does demonstrate is that a reassuring email reply can accompany a confirmed scam. What Evite says about the fake invitation scam We reached out to Evite about John's experience and asked whether the company was aware of this type of scam. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, Evite said: "We're not currently seeing a rise in phishing scams, however, staying aware is always important, which is why we're constantly monitoring and providing tools to help users spot the fakes at evite.com/blog/etiquette/how-to-spot-phishing-email-scam/ . The best way to tell the difference is that a scam is generic, but a real gathering today is highly specific. Real hosts are over-communicating, sharing everything from parking instructions and dress codes to very specific themes like 'Strawberry' or 'Western.' That level of detail is what makes a modern invite harder to fake and gives guests the confidence to say 'yes' without second-guessing. Evite advice? Check the details. If it just says 'You're invited' with a link, be cautious. A real Evite host today is telling you where to park and what to wear." Evite's advice is worth keeping in mind, although scammers can also create convincing invitations with specific event details. That's why it's important to take additional precautions before clicking an unexpected invitation. How to protect yourself from fake party invite scams A few changes to how you verify unexpected invitations can help prevent a suspicious email from becoming a much bigger problem. 1. Call your friend instead of sending another email If an invitation seems unusual, contact the sender using a phone number you already have. You can also reach out through another established communication channel, provided you have reason to trust that account. Avoid using phone numbers included in the suspicious invitation. A criminal could provide a fake contact number designed to make the story sound legitimate. 2. Treat unexpected login requests as warning signs Be cautious if an invitation asks you to enter your email password or share a security code before revealing event details. A phishing website may use those requests to steal account access. If you expect an invitation from a particular service, open its official app or visit its website directly. Check whether the invitation appears in your account rather than following an unfamiliar link. 3. Watch for unusual replies from people you know Pay attention if a familiar contact suddenly uses an unusual writing style or gives an answer that doesn't fit the conversation. Unexpected requests to click another link should make you even more cautious. However, don't rely entirely on spelling mistakes or punctuation. Criminals can write convincing messages, while legitimate emails may contain errors. The safest approach is to confirm the situation through another trusted method. 4. Use strong antivirus protection Fake invitations can sometimes lead to malicious downloads rather than stolen passwords. In certain attacks, criminals disguise remote access software as something you need to install to view an invitation. Strong antivirus software can help identify dangerous downloads and block known malicious websites on supported devices. Keep your operating system and security software updated so you receive the latest available protections. If you accidentally downloaded an invitation file, avoid opening it. Run a security scan using trusted software. If you entered login credentials on a suspicious website, change them through the legitimate service immediately. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 5. Check your Gmail account for suspicious settings If you suspect someone has accessed your Gmail account, review its settings for changes you didn't make. An attacker may use forwarding or automated email rules to interfere with incoming messages. On a computer, follow these steps: If you discover unfamiliar settings, investigate them and remove unauthorized changes. You should also secure your Google account and review recent sign-in activity. 6. Secure your email account before someone impersonates you A strong, unique password helps protect your email. You should also enable two-factor authentication or use a passkey where supported. Passkeys provide stronger protection against phishing because they are tied to legitimate websites or apps. Visit your Google Account security settings at myaccount.google.com/security to review recent activity and connected devices. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and sign out unfamiliar sessions. A password manager can help you avoid reusing passwords across accounts. That way, one exposed password is less likely to compromise another service. 7. Use a data removal service to limit your personal information online Scammers often use personal information found online to make fraudulent messages sound more convincing. Data brokers collect and sell details such as your email address, phone number and information about your family. A personal data removal service can help reduce that exposure by requesting that participating data brokers remove your information. Although no service can erase everything or prevent a friend's email account from being hacked, limiting what's available online may make it harder for criminals to personalize scams. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com 8. Report suspicious invitations and warn your contacts When you encounter a fraudulent invitation, use your email provider's phishing-reporting tools. In Gmail, open the suspicious message, select the three-dot menu and choose Report phishing . You can also report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If the message appears to come from a friend, contact that person using another trusted channel. They may need to secure their account and alert other people who received similar invitations. What to do if your friend confirms their email was hacked If your friend confirms that someone accessed their account, avoid interacting with the invitation. Save the suspicious message as evidence and report it to your email provider. You may also want to check whether you received any follow-up messages containing unfamiliar links. Encourage your friend to begin account recovery through their email provider's official website. They should review their account activity and remove unauthorized access. If the scammer sent invitations to other contacts, your friend should warn those people through a communication method they still control. For Gmail users, Google provides instructions for securing a hacked account. Acting quickly may help prevent additional messages from reaching trusted contacts. Kurt's key takeaways John's email made me reconsider a piece of advice I often give. I've always encouraged people to contact someone they know when a suspicious message arrives. I still believe that's smart advice, but how you reach that person is important. If their email account has been compromised, you could end up communicating with the scammer instead. Personally, I'd rather pick up the phone and call a number I already trust. I'm glad John trusted his instincts and followed up with his friend. He received a reply saying the invitation was legitimate, yet he kept questioning it. That extra effort helped him confirm the scam. We can't assume every strangely worded email comes from a hacker, but we also shouldn't ignore something that feels wrong. Scammers count on us trusting familiar names and email addresses. John's experience shows why a little extra verification can be worth the effort. articles.title: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts
articles.summary: Cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, but the company won’t take down its cameras and sometimes is reinstalling them.
articles.body: While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota’s city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city’s request. For over a month, the cameras remained up, and the city had received no acknowledgment from the company. So, Police Chief Eric Fadden took matters into his own hands and physically disconnected the cameras. “After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates,” Fadden told The Drive. Roughly 20 miles up the road, Dayton, Minnesota, is having its own issues with Flock. In this instance, the company acknowledged the city’s request and said it would take up to 60 days to remove the equipment. Despite this, Flock reconnected two cameras within the city limits without authorization, and following a specific request from the local police not to complete the work order. Dayton’s local government posted on Facebook: > On September 17, 2026, the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock. The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City’s direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization. Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith told The Verge, “We are proud of the impact our technology has had in Plymouth. We respect the city’s decision and are working with the customer to have the cameras removed.” This follows a similar ordeal in Illinois, where the company refused to take down cameras and uncovered cameras at Elgin Community College after the administration sought to cancel its contract. Update November 1st: Added comment from Flock.

articles.title: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is actually managing U.S. debt costs not inflation, economist says, as interest rates threaten to top GDP growth soon
articles.summary: "We’re not in hawkish or dovish land. What’s happening is yield curve management, which itself is a function of how precarious the U.S. debt picture is."
articles.body:
Trying to pin down Kevin Warsh as a hawk or a dove has been tricky with his statements and actions puzzling Wall Street.

As President Donald Trump's hand-picked Federal Reserve chairman, Warsh was expected to lean toward looser monetary policy. Then he declared that inflation was a "choice," suggesting a tougher approach.

Over the summer, he suggested looking at alternative inflation gauges and that the bond market would do some of the Fed's tightening work, hinting as less aggressive policy.

But he delivered a hawkish speech at the Jackson Hole conference in August, and led the Fed to a unanimous rate hike in September.

Last week, he held off on backing another rate hike, despite inflation heating up again, with his lack of explanation and refusal to offer any hints about the next policy decision producing an overall dovish effect.

But Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said asking whether Warsh is a hawk or a dove is the wrong question. Instead, he views all the mixed messages from the Fed chair through a different lens, arguing the hot inflation readings can't rationalize Warsh's statements.

"We're not in hawkish or dovish land. What's happening is yield curve management, which itself is a function of how precarious the U.S. debt picture is," Brooks wrote in a Substack post on Thursday.

That's because the surge in Treasury yields this year threatens to worsen the already-grim outlook for U.S. debt, which is now above $40 trillion in gross terms with publicly held debt at 100% of GDP.

In fiscal year 2026, which ended in September, the federal government's debt-interest costs topped $1 trillion, exceeding defense spending.

"The bottom line is that inflation and other macro data are secondary," Brooks added. "The twists and turns in Fed policy are about what's going on with long-term yields."

He suspects the Fed and Treasury Department are in a de facto accord to keep borrowing costs stable. Brooks pointed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's surprise announcement to buy back more long-term bonds, briefly lowering yields.

Bessent also intervened in the currency market to prop up the yen without Japan having to sell its holdings of U.S. debt, which would have lifted yields.

The actual effectiveness of these attempts at managing bond yields is a different story. Expectations for the Iran war to re-escalate have sent oil prices and yields higher. Signs that the U.S. economy is running hot have also raised inflation and rate forecasts.

But the U.S. also caught some breaks too. Fears that the AI boom, a major driver of GDP growth, will go bust have taken pressure off yields. France's political turmoil and fiscal dysfunction have sparked worries that it will trigger a debt crisis that spreads to other parts of the eurozone.

articles.title: Iowa’s cancer crisis could reshape the state’s biggest midterm races
articles.summary: Rising cancer rates and their potential link to farm pollution are causing a crisis in Iowa, throwing uncertainty into the midterm elections in a state that has shifted ruby-red in recent years. Iowa suffers from the second-highest rate of new cancer cases in the U.S., and it’s one of the few states where the number…
articles.body:
Rising cancer rates and their potential link to farm pollution are causing a crisis in Iowa, throwing uncertainty into the midterm elections in a state that has shifted ruby-red in recent years.

Iowa suffers from the second-highest rate of new cancer cases in the U.S., and it’s one of the few states where the number of cancer cases is rising. Across the state, the cancer crisis has become a major campaign topic.

Candidates from both parties have made tackling the environmental causes of cancer — and blaming “Big Ag” — a key part of their platforms. It’s an attack that previously would have been unheard of from Republicans in the Corn Belt hub.

The state has a series of blockbuster races this year, including the governor’s contest between Zach Lahn (R) and Rob Sand (D), the Senate race between Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) and several competitive House races.

Lahn, in an unusual move for a Republican, is not only leaning into the cancer issue but also vowing to clean Iowa’s water and regulate chemicals if he’s elected.

“We have the fastest rate of new cancer anywhere in the country, number one. If you move out of the state of Iowa, to, say, a state like Nevada, your chance of getting cancer any given year goes down by 40 percent,” Lahn said during a “Face the Nation” interview earlier this month .

The focus on cancer and the role of Big Agriculture shows the influence the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has had in the state.

MAHA principles, especially those that push for clean water and food at the expense of pesticides and farm profits, are often at odds with the Republican Party’s historically probusiness agenda , especially in agriculture-heavy Iowa.

Karen Kedrowski, a professor of political science at Iowa State University, said Lahn discussing cancer is significant because it is such a departure from traditional Republican views. But it speaks to the massive scale of the issue for voters.

“When you start talking about cancer, everybody knows somebody, or a friend of a friend, or someone who has had cancer,” Kedrowski said. “The cancer piece really becomes salient because it’s so common and kind of top of mind.”

In a year where Iowa Democrats feel they have their best shot in more than two decades at winning the governorship, healthcare and the environment are in the spotlight.

Republicans are hoping Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his MAHA agenda can bring voters to the polls.

Timothy Hagle, a political science professor at the University of Iowa, said voters who support the agriculture industry, a frequent MAHA target, may not be likely to “all of a sudden flip and support the Democrats in whatever race we’re talking about.”

But, he said, Kennedy may be persuasive for voters without strong partisan ties.

“The idea may be that RFK Jr. …. can maybe appeal to more of those no-party voters,” Hagle told The Hill.

MAHA threw its support behind Lahn early, helping him defeat Rep. Randy Feenstra, an established politician who was endorsed by Trump.

Lahn was the first candidate endorsed by MAHA Action, the Kennedy-aligned advocacy group run by Tony Lyons, Kennedy’s book publisher and a key ally.

Kennedy has made repeated visits to Iowa to boost GOP candidates, most recently headlining a MAHA rally featuring Lahn and Joe Mitchell, a candidate for the House seat being vacated by Hinson as she runs for Senate.

“I love Zach, because we need to figure out a way to feed ourselves in this country, make this country the breadbasket of the world without degrading our soils and without poisoning our children,” Kennedy said during the rally.

Aside from cancer and chemicals, Lahn has also adopted other MAHA principles: He’s promised to end vaccine mandates in schools and ban the COVID-19 vaccine.

However, in Iowa, environmental issues do not fall neatly along party lines. For example, Chris Jones, a Democratic candidate for Iowa agriculture secretary, is also running on a platform of clean water.

“This cancer issue is resonating with people, and almost everyone has a story here of a family member or someone else that has met an early demise,” Jones told The Hill earlier this year.

And while he certainly has differences with Lahn, Jones said that having a Republican also speaking out about water quality “makes me look less like a renegade.”

Jones has been endorsed by democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), but he also has a MAHA tie in his finance director, Dave Murphy, who also worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign.

And Jones’s opponent, incumbent Mike Naig (R), used to work for Monsanto, whose Roundup weedkiller has become a prime target of the MAHA movement.

Murphy told The Hill that even with MAHA candidates in the race, “Democrats have won” on issues of water quality. However, he thinks that Lahn may “keep some of the votes that would run from Feenstra … to Rob Sand.”

The MAHA movement is not a singular bloc, and there are different factions with priorities that don’t necessarily translate neatly into partisan camps. Some members prioritize changes to the food supply, others want tighter chemical and pesticide regulation, and some want to eliminate vaccine mandates.

The newfound focus on the issue could create an opening for Democrats and MAHA-aligned Republicans alike — and it could give the Trump administration extra incentive to have Kennedy make its case.

“The Republican Party has taken the rural vote for granted,” said Jeff Hutt, who worked on Kennedy’s presidential campaign. “Now that Republican policies, through support of Big Ag, through use of pesticides, [are] starting to affect these rural communities negatively, I think you’re going to see a shift in the Republican Party about how they treat these issues.”

Meanwhile, Democrat-aligned groups hope that voters will tip in their favor in part because of issues such as clean water and healthcare.

“Republicans have had a chance to show up and deliver on promises from everything from lowering cost to the things that they said they would do around MAHA voters’ concerns, and I think that they’ve failed miserably,” said Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of campaigns at the League of Conservation Voters Victory Fund.

“We have powerful testimonials as part of our communications to voters, and these are Iowans who are really concerned about their water quality and the efforts to chip away at it while they’re taking corporate contributions from these companies,” Schreiber said.

As one example, the group is running an ad targeting Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) on votes she has taken on water pollution, healthcare cuts and cuts to cancer research.

Tuesday’s midterms also come amid a backdrop of other political debates, including broad issues of affordability and agriculture-specific matters related to high diesel prices, which raise costs for farmers. That, too, could drive voters toward Democrats as the Trump administration’s war in Iran and foreign tariffs have exacerbated the problem.

Still, Hutt said he views the governor’s race itself as a victory for the MAHA movement.

“The fact that you have two candidates running for the governor of Iowa who have embraced MAHA principles almost exactly, with the exception of vaccines, I think that is more a statement about the success of the movement than whichever candidate wins the election,” he said.

“In my mind, MAHA has already won this election. It doesn’t matter who comes out with the most votes at the end.”
