articles.title: Wall Street Braces for Biggest Treasury Sales Overhaul in Years
articles.summary: After Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent surprised dealers with his willingness to intervene in the bond market to drive down yields in recent months, Wall Str...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- After Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent surprised dealers with his willingness to intervene in the bond market to drive down yields in recent months, Wall Street is now girding for the biggest revamp in guidance for US Treasuries issuance since early 2024.

Many dealers expect the Treasury to alter the guidance in its quarterly policy statement, which for more than two years has laid out steady plans for note and bond issuance. A shift in Wednesday's announcement could pave the way for potential cuts in 2027 to sales of the longest-dated debt, balanced by bigger auctions of bills and shorter-term notes.

Some are prepping for more drastic action. Citigroup Inc. predicts the Treasury will announce cuts to sales of 20- and 30-year bonds starting this month — effectively violating the guidance issued in the last so-called quarterly refunding statement. Just one week after that last plan, Bessent unexpectedly ramped up buybacks of outstanding securities, in a move seen as a reaction to a surge in yields.

"Buybacks are too small to really move the needle," April LaRusse, head of investment specialists at Insight Investment, said in an interview. She put it simply: "if you're running the Treasury and your main power is issuance, if you don't like where the yields are, you adjust your issuance."

The proviso for any major shakeup this week is that yields have retreated since longer-dated rates hit their highest in more than two decades in early October. Still, 30-year bonds on Friday were trading with yields above 5.30%, around levels seen in mid-August when Bessent intervened with his expanded buyback program.

Another consideration: relying even more heavily on bills, which mature in up to a year, to meet expanding funding needs at some point is bound at some point to test the appetite of investors. With rapidly maturing bills having to be refunded constantly, the US now auctions in excess of half a trillion dollars in any given week, leaving the Treasury exposed to sudden swings. Last week, officials sold a record $839 billion.

"Guidance is more likely than immediate action" to alter issuance strategy, said Phoebe White, head of US rates strategy at UBS Group AG. Still, the Treasury's recent "unconventional" behavior does "increase the odds that Treasury actions continue to deviate from historical precedent," she said.

articles.title: More European supermarkets are getting their freezers hacked
articles.summary: Grocery stores across Europe have been hit by another wave of suspected cyberattacks, reporting sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers.﻿
articles.body: Grocery stores across Europe have been hit by another wave of suspected cyberattacks, reporting sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers. Major supermarket chains across Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg, and Estonia were affected, according to local reports shared by Bloomberg and Reuters. One Ica Kvantum store in Sweden said on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked overnight, with temperatures remotely raised to 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit). In a statement to Business Insider, a spokesperson at Swedish supermarket chain Coop also confirmed that “unauthorized actors were able to access and tamper with the cooling systems at a small fraction of our stores.” Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said an “IT incident” was responsible for adjusting the temperature of refrigeration units in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg. The full scale of the incident has yet to be confirmed. Many modern supermarket fridges and freezers are connected to the internet to support remote maintenance and system failure alerts, but the increasing number of these suspected hacks is raising concerns around how security flaws can impact food supply chains. This latest incident follows an apparent cyberattack that targeted hundreds of French supermarket refrigerators last month, with the resulting food spoilage estimated to be worth millions of euros, along with a string of US military base freezer malfunctions also suspected to be the result of a cyberattack.

articles.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock private chats with a PIN
articles.summary: OpenAI's new locked chats feature lets you protect ChatGPT conversations with a PIN, Face ID or Touch ID, but there are key privacy limitations.
articles.body: Ever handed someone your phone or let them use your computer to show them something, then suddenly worried about what else they might see? Maybe you've been using ChatGPT to work through a personal issue or plan a surprise for someone. Your conversation history can reveal quite a bit. Now, OpenAI is giving you a way to keep certain conversations out of sight. The company just introduced Locked Chats, a new feature that lets you protect individual ChatGPT conversations with a four-digit PIN. On supported devices, you can also use Face ID, Touch ID or your phone's unlock method. That sounds reassuring, especially as more people turn to artificial intelligence for personal advice. However, there are a few privacy limitations worth understanding before you start locking everything down. Here's how the feature works and how to set it up. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay and downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN What are ChatGPT Locked Chats? OpenAI's new Locked Chats feature allows you to protect selected conversations without deleting them. Once you lock a chat, it moves into a separate area under Projects > Locked chats. The conversation disappears from your regular chat history, pinned chats and standard search results. Its title and contents stay behind your PIN until you choose to open them. You can even continue the conversation later without moving it back into your regular history. Think about how useful that could be if you share a computer with your spouse or occasionally let someone use your phone. Perhaps you're researching an anniversary surprise and don't want the details popping up in your sidebar. Now, you have a way to keep that conversation separate. There's one important detail if you already use ChatGPT Projects. Locking a conversation removes it from its original project. As a result, the conversation loses access to that project's instructions, files and memory. Even if you unlock it later, the conversation returns to your regular history rather than its previous project. The feature is rolling out gradually to ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users. It works on the web, in the iPhone and Android apps and in the new ChatGPT desktop apps for Mac and Windows. OpenAI says ChatGPT for Healthcare does not support Locked Chats. How to lock a ChatGPT conversation with a PIN You can lock an existing conversation in a few steps. The process is similar whether you're using ChatGPT on your computer, iPhone, Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel. Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked. Your conversation will move into Locked chats. The PIN belongs to your OpenAI account, so you can use the same PIN across supported devices where you're signed in. Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked. META AI LAUNCHES PRIVATE INCOGNITO CHAT How to use Face ID or Touch ID for ChatGPT Locked Chats Typing a PIN every time you want to open a personal conversation can get tiresome. Fortunately, OpenAI supports biometric authentication on compatible iPhones and device authentication on supported Android phones. How to use Face ID or Touch ID on iPhone You can now use supported biometric authentication to access locked conversations on that iPhone. Your four-digit account PIN remains available as a backup. How to use device unlock on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel users follow the same steps inside the ChatGPT app. The available authentication method depends on your phone and its settings. Once enabled, you can use your supported device unlock method to access protected conversations. Depending on your phone, that may include fingerprint recognition or another available authentication method. This setting applies only to the device where you enable it. Turning on device authentication on your Galaxy or Pixel does not automatically enable it on another phone. How to open a locked ChatGPT conversation Once you've protected a chat, you'll probably want to return to it. Fortunately, OpenAI keeps your locked conversations in one dedicated location. You can continue chatting as you normally would. Opening the conversation temporarily gives you access without permanently removing its protection. You can also start a brand-new conversation directly inside Locked chats. After opening that area with your PIN, simply enter a new message. It will remain in the protected section. However, there's a limitation worth knowing. OpenAI doesn't allow you to archive, pin, move or share a conversation while it's locked. You'll need to permanently unlock it before using those options. Anyone who can open a locked conversation can also copy its contents. Will ChatGPT lock your conversations again automatically? Yes, although the timing depends on your device. On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel, OpenAI says access ends automatically after you've been away from a locked chat or the Locked chats area for one minute. The same one-minute rule applies when the app runs in the background. On the web, refreshing the page or closing the tab ends access. The desktop and web versions also relock after you've been away from the authorized window. If you want to secure everything immediately, select Lock now. There's another detail worth knowing. A conversation may remain visible in the browser tab immediately after you lock it. Similarly, another device that's already running ChatGPT might temporarily display an older conversation title until it refreshes. So, check your screen before handing over your device. How to move a locked ChatGPT conversation back to regular history You may eventually decide that a conversation no longer needs extra protection. You can return it to your normal history without deleting its contents. The conversation returns to your regular history and can eventually appear in ordinary search results again. The privacy limits of ChatGPT Locked Chats Here's where I want you to pay close attention. Locking a conversation can stop someone casually browsing your chat history. However, OpenAI makes clear that Locked Chats do not provide end-to-end encryption or create a separate encrypted vault. The company also says locking a chat does not change how long it retains your information. Your existing Improve the model for everyone setting remains unchanged, too. Memory introduces another consideration. If ChatGPT remembered something before you locked a conversation, that information can still exist in regular Memory. Once the chat is locked, new information remembered from subsequent messages stays within the Locked Chats memory area. Other locked conversations can use that information, but regular chats do not receive those new memories automatically. Locked chats can also draw on existing regular Memory when it's enabled. There's also a potential surprise involving shared links. If you previously shared a conversation through a link, locking it does not revoke that link. Anyone with the existing link may still access the content that was previously shared. You must delete the shared link separately to stop that access. Files come with their own limitations. Documents and other files uploaded or created inside a locked conversation receive the same protection as the chat itself. However, files already stored elsewhere in ChatGPT's Space or brought in from connected services keep their existing access permissions. Locking a conversation won't automatically protect those separate files. For workplace accounts, existing organizational retention and compliance policies still apply. OpenAI says Enterprise and Edu conversation logs can include locked chats through its compliance tools. Workspace administrators cannot unlock your chats or reset your PIN, but authorized compliance systems may still access applicable conversation data. These are important limitations if you're discussing financial information or other highly personal subjects. I would still avoid uploading passwords, Social Security numbers or complete banking credentials to a general ChatGPT conversation. How to stop ChatGPT from using your new chats for AI training If you're concerned about how OpenAI handles your conversations, there's another privacy setting you should review. Turning off Improve the model for everyone prevents your new conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. These instructions apply to personal ChatGPT accounts. OpenAI says content from ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces is not used to train its models by default. Here's how to do it. On the ChatGPT website On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel Your new conversations will no longer be used for model training after you turn off this setting. They can still remain in your chat history, so you'll need Locked Chats or another option to keep them out of view. For additional privacy controls across other AI services, see my guide on how to opt out of AI data collection in popular apps. ChatGPT Locked Chats vs. Temporary Chat: Which should you use? OpenAI already offers a feature called Temporary Chat, which serves a different purpose. Temporary Chats don't appear in your regular history or create new memories. OpenAI also excludes them from model training while they remain temporary. However, the company may retain temporary conversations for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Depending on your settings, a Temporary Chat can also use existing personalization information. Locked Chats make more sense when you want to save a conversation and return to it later without leaving it exposed in your normal history. You can keep adding messages, and the conversation stays behind your PIN. So, if you're having a one-time discussion you don't need to save, Temporary Chat may be the better choice. If you're working through something personal over several days, Locked Chats gives you a way to maintain that conversation with additional access protection. What happens if you forget your ChatGPT PIN? This is one detail I really don't want you to overlook. Resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes all your locked chats, along with memories stored only within those chats and files or other content protected only by the previous PIN. OpenAI says the deletion cannot be undone. Even its support team cannot recover that protected content. If you remember your current PIN and simply want to change it, you can do so without losing your conversations. How to change your ChatGPT PIN If you've forgotten your PIN, you can also reset it from Settings > Security and login > Account PIN. However, you'll need to verify your identity and confirm the permanent deletion of your protected chats and associated content before creating a replacement PIN. One more thing: OpenAI doesn't allow every conversation to be locked. The exclusions include Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats and conversations created from shared links. Chats involving scheduled tasks, meeting recordings or background tasks are also excluded. The same applies to conversations with responses saved as project sources. Some Health, Codex and Work conversations have additional restrictions. If the Lock chat option doesn't appear, your conversation may not qualify. Kurt's key takeaways I like that OpenAI is finally giving people more control over which conversations appear when someone opens ChatGPT. As AI becomes a place where people work through personal decisions, there's a real need for some discretion. Being able to hand someone your phone without exposing an entire conversation history is a useful improvement. Still, I would treat Locked Chats as a convenience and access-control feature rather than a guarantee of confidentiality. The four-digit PIN helps keep curious eyes away, but your broader privacy depends on the information you share and the settings you've chosen. And that leaves me wondering whether OpenAI should eventually offer something stronger for conversations people consider deeply private. Would you trust ChatGPT with your most personal conversations if they were protected by a PIN, or should OpenAI offer stronger privacy protections before you feel comfortable sharing? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Federal probe launched into deadly Florida plane crash
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has launched an investigation into a deadly plane crash in Florida that killed all people onboard. Around 12:50 p.m. EST, a Learjet 60 crashed in a neighborhood near Cresthaven, Fla., after departing from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. The flight was en route…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has launched an investigation into a deadly plane crash in Florida that killed all people onboard.

Around 12:50 p.m. EST, a Learjet 60 crashed in a neighborhood near Cresthaven, Fla., after departing from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. The flight was en route to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). All nine people on the jet died in the crash.

Duffy in a statement called the incident a “horrific tragedy” and noted the FAA “is sending a team to the scene to support the @NTSB’s investigation.”

“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost,” he wrote on social platform X. “@FAANews & @USDOT are closely monitoring this crash and will share updates as we learn more.”

The NTSB said on X that investigators were sent to the crash site and arrived Sunday night and Monday morning. A press conference will be held in West Palm Beach.

Videos showing the jet moments before it slammed into the ground went viral online.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said there were no reports of anyone killed on the ground in what he called a “cataclysmic plane crash,” The Associated Press reported.

“It was a ​big-time tragedy that happened,” DeSantis said at a press conference close to ⁠the crash site in Lake Worth Beach, according to Reuters . “When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like ​a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.”

The plane traveled east at 35,000 feet when pilots reported turbulence and icing as the plane faced pounding rain that caused the National Weather Service to issue a flood watch on the ground below.

Pilots requested to climb another 2,000 feet before it dived 10,000 feet per minute, 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute at speeds beyond what it was designed for, according to the AP, which cited air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.

One of the pilots issued distress calls after declaring an emergency, with one of them saying the plane was going to crash. About 35 seconds after the emergency declaration, a pilot quickly said from the cockpit, “We’re out of time,” Reuters reported. The plane banked sharply to the right before it crashed into the ground.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores ​said during the press conference that the accident left a “massive crater” near a mobile home park, prompting the evacuation of around 600 people in the area.

The crash was in Greenacres, Fla., around 10 miles from President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.

articles.title: A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe's supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries | TechCrunch
articles.summary: This is the second wave of cyberattacks to hit supermarket refrigerators in a month, spoiling food and disrupting supplies.
articles.body:
A second wave of cyberattacks is suspected to have hit supermarket refrigerators across Europe, causing fridges to increase temperatures and spoil food at dozens of stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks overnight, with one Belgian company that operates Delhaize’s systems saying that the hackers had changed the settings to defrost, per Reuters . Stores have experienced heavy food losses from the cyberattacks, forcing supermarkets to throw out goods that had defrosted or were otherwise no longer consumable.

The cyberattacks follow earlier refrigerator hacks across in France last month that caused food spoilage at hundreds of supermarkets by deliberately raising the temperature on the units. Security researchers said that the cause of the hacks were internet-connected refrigerators made by Danish company Danfoss, which was no longer providing security updates. Security company Claroty warned back in August that those refrigerator units were at risk of remote hacks and outages.

The freezer hacks underscore how cyberattacks can have real-world effects, including on the food supply chain, often as a result of weak or overlooked cybersecurity practices. In 2025, a cyberattack on food distributor giant UNFI resulted in food shortages and empty shelves at grocery stores and supermarkets across the United States.

U.S. Department of Defense officials are reportedly investigating whether freezer units on military bases were hacked by Iran-backed hackers. Iranian hackers were also blamed for cyberattacks targeting U.S. water providers earlier this year.

articles.title: Could data center backlash flip Florida?
articles.summary: David Jolly, Florida’s Democratic nominee for governor is counting on data centers to break the GOP’s decades-long hold on the state.
articles.body: Patti Zirhut, a lifelong Republican, has been studying her ballot for weeks. Zirhut eagerly voted for President Donald Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024, but she isn’t toeing the party line this year. “My ballot is all mixed up,” she says. She’s voting for some Republicans, some independents, and even a few Democrats. Zirhut remains undecided on a few races, but of one thing she is absolutely certain: “I will not vote for Byron Donalds,” she tells me. “No way will I ever vote for him.” Donalds, the Republican nominee in Florida’s gubernatorial election, has Trump’s endorsement, the party’s backing, and $148 million in campaign funds, much of it from the tech industry. It’s this latest point that particularly rankles Zirhut, an organizer with a group called No Data Center Hernando County, whose purpose is summed up in its name. Donalds has been a vocal supporter of the controversial developments — a fact that may now cost him votes, even among members of his own party. I first met Zirhut in August at a small protest in the rural community of Spring Hill, Florida. Back then, Donalds was the front-runner in a crowded Republican primary, and Zirhut told me she wouldn’t vote for him if he won. Now Donalds is the nominee in a race that is much closer than anyone anticipated, and Zirhut is sticking to her word. “I’m disgusted with all these dirty politics,” she tells me. She’s thinking about voting for Donalds’ Democratic opponent, former Rep. David Jolly. Jolly, a former Republican who left the party in 2018, is now hoping to win over newly disgruntled conservatives like Zirhut — and his stance on data centers may help him do it. In Florida, the opposition to data centers “is more intense among Republicans than it is among Democrats,” Jolly tells The Verge, “because it is a reflection of the outsized influence and control of Big Tech and Big Data in a world where people are worried about surveillance, whether it’s AI or development encroaching on their land and their freedom.” When it comes to data centers, the differences between Donalds and Jolly couldn’t be more stark. Jolly has traveled to Virginia’s Loudoun County, also known as Data Center Alley, to “see what massive hyperscale data centers really do to a community.” Donalds has said he wants to “make Florida the financial capital of the world.” Jolly has promised to implement a one-year moratorium on data center developments. Donalds has said he wants to welcome the tech industry — including data center developers — to the Sunshine State. “There ain’t no bans coming,” Donalds said in August. “But it sounds good on TV, or it sounds good on social media.” Donalds has since moderated his stance on data centers, trying to appeal to the 68 percent of Floridians who say they oppose the developments in their communities. “This is an opportunity you rarely see in politics for candidates to both lead and follow,” Jolly says. “If 70 percent of the state is saying ‘Don’t do it,’ the job is to listen to voters, not to tell voters they’re wrong. But there are policy reasons, as well, to lead in this moment.” Jolly rattled off a litany of reasons to slow down, if not altogether halt, data center development in Florida: air and noise pollution; the public health effects on people who live near data centers’ on-site power plants; and environmental concerns including water use, an issue he acknowledged is partly mitigated by the move to closed-loop air cooling. He also pointed to the rapid development of AI technology, which is advancing so quickly that facilities built today “may well be functionally obsolete in the next 10 years.” Donalds is quick to point out that his running mate, state Sen. Bryan Ávila, sponsored a bill regulating new data center projects that requires them to pay their fair share for water and electricity. And he’s emphasized that these developments ultimately aren’t the governor’s purview. “When it comes to data centers and local control, local governments are going to have the final say,” Donalds recently told CBS News. “Governors don’t issue building permits; local governments do. So if a local community does not want a data center, then no data centers.” But Jolly has saddled his opponent with a nickname that sums up their differences on the issue: “Data Center Donalds.” Donalds’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Raul Alfonso, the chair of Watchdogs of Fort Meade, a community group fighting a $2.6 billion hyperscale data center development in deep-red Polk County, said his group has reached out to candidates in the lead-up to the election. Earlier this year, Watchdogs of Fort Meade received what Alfonso describes as a “form letter” from both Donalds and from Ron DeSantis, Florida’s current Republican governor. “It was basically, ‘We have to trust that your local city commissioners and your local city representatives will do the right thing,’” he says. The group hasn’t heard back from Jolly — which doesn’t bother Alfonso much, given Jolly’s promised moratorium. James Fishback, the controversial Republican contender who ended up with 10 percent of the primary vote, was the first to respond. Bobby Williams, a Republican candidate who garnered just 4.1 percent of the vote, has attended several events. Angie Nixon, the Democrat running to unseat Sen. Ashley Moody, hosted a town hall in Fort Meade to discuss residents’ opposition to the data centers. For Alfonso, the difference comes down to a willingness to hear locals’ concerns. Nixon, a Democratic Socialist, has little in common with the far-right Fishback, but both have engaged with the locals fighting the Fort Meade data center in a way Donalds hasn’t. “There are a lot of people that were deep-red individuals who voted party line all the way, who are looking at flopping over to somebody who will actually take the concerns of the citizens more seriously,” Alfonso says. Alfonso’s voting history skews conservative — he voted for Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024 — but he was a registered independent until this year, when he switched his affiliation to Republican to vote for Williams in the primary. Williams, a pastor who had not previously run for office, has since endorsed Jolly. “The Republican Party, they kind of selected their nominee. They had their guy from the get-go: Donalds,” Williams tells me. “Big corporations are obviously buying a lot of these seats. They’re buying the governor’s role.” For Williams, data center developers are the latest in a long list of outsiders that want to have their way with Florida. If he wins, Jolly will be the first Democratic governor Florida has elected in 28 years. The polls are close. One recent survey conducted by the University of North Florida put Jolly just two points behind Donalds, within the 2.8 percent margin of error. Donalds has several advantages over Jolly, not least of which is money. Jolly has raised $22 million to Donalds’ $148 million. There’s also the fact that Florida, once a swing state, now has nearly 2 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, in part because of DeSantis’ response to the covid-19 pandemic. The fact that Republicans currently lead Democrats in early voting may suggest that the state is unlikely to flip. But some of those Republicans, including Zirhut, are wary of Donald’s support for — and from — the tech industry, and are voting accordingly. Donalds has received $5 million from Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC whose funders include executives of OpenAI, Palantir, and Andreessen Horowitz. As vocal as data center opponents may be, these developments aren’t Florida voters’ main issue. Poll after poll has shown that in Florida and elsewhere, the cost of living is top of mind for voters of all political orientations. But Jolly says the mass opposition to data centers is a manifestation of voters’ broader concerns. “It’s almost a physical metaphor for anxieties around, ‘What is the future of work? What’s the future of wages? What does this mean for security and privacy for myself and for my kids?’” Jolly says. The huge sums of money spent on the governor’s race, he adds, are a testament to economic inequality in a state with an ever-rising cost of living. “In a state like Florida with unlimited money, where people feel like they’ve lost their political and economic power and voice, the deepest-pocketed special interests — be it tech, data, utilities — are able to capture our politicians and decision-making.”

The job cuts will affect around 300 of Squarespace’s 1,800 employees. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth,” Seedman says. “We are grateful for the contributions of our departing colleagues and are providing comprehensive support to help them through the transition.” Seedman adds that impacted employees will receive 16 weeks of base pay and healthcare benefits into May 2027. articles.title: Treasury Yields Extend Past Month’s Slide as Oil Prices Tumble
articles.summary: Treasuries rose, building on their biggest monthly advance in more than two years, as tumbling oil prices eased concern about inflation pressure leading to a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasuries rose, building on their biggest monthly advance in more than two years, as tumbling oil prices eased concern about inflation pressure leading to additional Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes.

Ten- to 30-year maturities led gains, with yields for those tenors declining four to six basis points and reaching the lowest levels since September.

Shorter-dated debt rose less as lower oil prices helped stabilize US stocks. Equities weakness concentrated in large technology company shares benefited the Treasury market last month as investors piled into lower-risk assets.

"The historical negative correlation between bonds and equities seems to have returned over the past month, and the gains today could be related to investors looking to protect further downside in equities," said Steven Zeng, an interest-rate strategist at Deutsche Bank. The oil price slide "also supports Treasury yields to move lower."

The US 10-year yield declined as much as five basis points to under 4.88%, the lowest level since Sept. 10.

Benchmark oil prices fell more than 7% Monday on hopes for renewed talks to end the Middle East war the US started in February. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell as much as 7.5%.

Fed policymakers raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 after rising oil prices caused inflation to accelerate. Traders continue to price in at least two more quarter-point hikes by the end of next year, however the cumulative amount of expected tightening has declined over the past month.

Short-term Treasury yields falling less than longer-term ones "is likely a consequence of the sharp post-FOMC steepening move" following last week's decision to leave rates unchanged, said Dhiraj Narula, US rates strategist at HSBC's US investment bank.

The move also reflects "questions around potential long-end Treasury supply cuts" that US officials may answer at Wednesday's quarterly discussion of their borrowing strategy.

articles.title: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
articles.summary: The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against Brave ​Software over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls.
articles.body: The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against the company that makes the Brave web browser over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls, as reported by Reuters. According to a complaint filed by the New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index.” The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to “respond to specific user queries,” or both. Brave has allegedly provided “stolen copyrighted content” to “many” AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Brave also promotes “hundreds of top publishers” as being accessible through its “Paywall blocker” feature in its browser. “Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies,” the complaint says. “On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers’ paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave’s access to the Publishers’ websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers’ copyrighted content.” “While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement to The Verge. “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world.” “AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” says Steven Lieberman, the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the other three publications. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.” Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI, and Cohere didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. “The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” says Jesse Dwyer, Perplexity’s chief communications officer. Update, November 2nd: Clarified that one lawsuit was filed by New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, not the companies that run them. Also added a statement from the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of those publications.

articles.title: Snap settles social media addiction case, ending bellwether trial
articles.summary: Snap Inc., the parent company of social media app Snapchat, has settled claims alleging the platform was intentionally designed to be addictive for young users, ending the bellwether trial two days before opening arguments in Los Angeles. The settlement, announced Monday by the legal teams for plaintiffs “SJ” and “KDB,” follows similar deals reached last…
articles.body:
Snap Inc., the parent company of social media app Snapchat, has settled claims alleging the platform was intentionally designed to be addictive for young users, ending the bellwether trial two days before opening arguments in Los Angeles.

The settlement, announced Monday by the legal teams for plaintiffs “SJ” and “KDB,” follows similar deals reached last month with tech giant Meta, which was a codefendant in the trial up until Friday. The terms of Snap Inc.’s settlement are confidential, attorneys added, and the social media company said the parties were “pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner.”

The settlements allow both Snap Inc. and Meta to avoid another high-profile trial this year, which was expected to feature Snap Inc. CEO Evan Spiegel taking the stand in court for the first time. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram head Adam Mosseri were also expected to testify.

The trial, which originally consolidated two cases, began last week in Los Angeles County Superior Court with jury selection.

KDB, a woman from Mississippi, argued her use of social media platforms Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm.

SJ, a teenager from Illinois, said she started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing app features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscores” along with filters and push notifications. Her attorneys alleged these features played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat.

Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Emily Jeffcott, representing KDB, celebrated the settlement Monday, stating they are “proud to have achieved justice for our bellweather clients so far.”

“Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal,” they said in a statement shared Monday.

Joseph VanZandt, an attorney for SJ at the Beasley Allen Law Firm, said the settlement with Snap Inc. secures “real results” for SJ and her family.

“This litigation has always been about making social media safer for kids, and nothing about these resolutions slows that work,” VanZandt said. “We will be back in a courtroom in March, and we will keep going until these platforms are safe for the children who use them.”

A spokesperson for Snap Inc. said Snapchat was “built to encourage real conversations with real friends.”

“We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community,” the spokesperson said.

The next group of bellweather cases are slated for trial in March 2027.

The settlement comes just days after Meta reached an agreement with KDB on Friday. SJ settled her claims the previous week.

articles.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
articles.summary: Ford announced a new privacy pledge vowing never to sell driver data to third-party brokers, seeking an edge after GM’s multimillion-dollar settlement.
articles.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

articles.title: Fitness program cut transplant waitlist death risk by half, study finds
articles.summary: Patients who improved their fitness while waiting for a transplant were about 50% less likely to die before receiving an organ, researchers found.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Being a candidate for a transplant can be a scary proposition, but new research suggests patients who improve their fitness while awaiting the procedure may lower their risk of death.

A study conducted by Northwestern University and published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology found that frailty can be significantly improved through a personalized, physician-led fitness program.

“It doesn’t matter how severe their disease is,” Northwestern’s Dr. Andres Duarte-Rojo said. “If they exercise and do what we ask them to do, they see a major improvement in their fitness and reduce their mortality risk before transplantation.”

Duarte-Rojo and his team analyzed nearly 1,300 adult patients who were evaluated for liver transplantation between 2018 and 2022 at the University of Pittsburgh’s transplant center. Of the 1,300 participants, 355 were enrolled in the prehabilitation program.

Researchers tracked changes using three measures: grip strength, chair stands and the ability to maintain three balance positions. They found that 64 percent of patients in the prehabilitation program improved their scores, and those whose scores increased by at least 0.4 points had about a 50 percent lower risk of dying while waiting for a transplant.

“You don’t send these patients to the gym to lift 100 pounds,” Duarte-Rojo added. “You have to start low and progress slowly. But we find that the frailest ones often improve the most.”

According to the United Network of Organ Sharing , roughly 100,000 people in the United States are waiting for a transplant. Depending on the organ needed, average wait times can range from a few months to several years.

articles.title: Germany says lawmakers' iPhones may have been hacked with spyware | TechCrunch
articles.summary: German lawmakers and a filmmaker are among the people who received notifications from Apple warning that their phones may have been hacked.
articles.body:
The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending out notifications warning victims that their iPhones may have been hacked.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity office, known as the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that it had become aware that members of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, and other unnamed notable individuals had received warnings from Apple that they may have been targeted by cyberattacks.

Per the Financial Times , German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the government in Berlin was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” but he did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether German chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them.

Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to people it thinks may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information from their phones. This spyware often relies on zero-click exploits , which can hack individuals almost invisibly as they don’t require a victim to click on a link or open a file.

Apple does not attribute attacks to specific governments or say whether someone’s phone has actually been compromised. For that reason, the BSI said that anyone who receives an Apple threat notification “should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.”

Others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple. Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, said in a post on X that he received a new threat notification warning that Apple had detected “another attack against your device,” after an earlier spyware attack targeted him in 2021.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

The episode highlights again the murky business behind a growing number of attacks against members of civil society. Governments rarely build these tools themselves. Many buy them from private vendors, often called “mercenary spyware” makers, the best known being Israel’s NSO Group, which sells the controversial Pegasus spyware. Germany’s own central federal law agency, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019.

articles.summary: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Parts of a business jet appear to have broken off before the aircraft crashed in South Florida and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said Monday. Video recorded by a passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the…
articles.body:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Parts of a business jet appear to have broken off before the aircraft crashed in South Florida and erupted into a ball of flames , killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said Monday.

Video recorded by a passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

“Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. “I’ve always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today.”

National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that the aircraft appeared to start breaking up before it made impact and that he expects parts of the plane will be found far away.

“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact,” Chapman said. “We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.”

Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel G. Flores said at the news conference that the county “doesn’t have a clue” when residents living around crash site will be able to return home.

There were around 77 mobile homes in the area and residents of those homes have been evacuated to a shelter, Flores said.

“Our concern right now is clearing the scene so that our residents can get back to normal,” Flores said. “We don’t really have a timeline as to when they are going to be able to comb through all the evidence and do everything they need to do, and that leaves our community looking for answers.”

The Bahamas-bound jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. Airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office declined to discuss the death investigation, saying it is still in early stages.

Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times that her daughter, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, was one of the pilots. She earned her pilot’s license in 2023 while a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School in Florida, local news reports said at the time .

Her pilot’s license showed she had the rating to fly that model of Learjet but not to be in command of the flight.

Her father, Allan Filgueiras, told The Associated Press he wasn’t prepared to speak about the crash.

Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter asked for sympathy for the crash victims.

“Please keep them in your thoughts and prayers,” she said.

Pilot reported turbulence and ice, then the jet’s rapid descent

The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (11,000 meters) when the pilot started to report problems.

The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net . Rain pounded the region on Sunday.

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.

The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters) and then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.

“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.

“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed. Moments later, the pilot said: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”

Video shows the plane banking sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.

“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”

Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California; Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; and Philip Marcelo in East Meadow, New York, contributed.

articles.body:
President Trump on Monday touted a new drop in oil prices during his closing pitch to voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

International benchmark Brent crude was trading at $104 Monday afternoon, down from $112 earlier in the day. U.S. benchmark WTI was trading at about $96 per barrel, down from nearly $103.

The price drop came amid some signs of positivity in talks with Iran. Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. agreed to meet certain conditions, but it is unclear if the U.S. will meet those conditions. There has also been talk in Washington of new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

The war has periodically seen closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping lane, as well as higher costs to transport oil even when ships have been allowed to pass through. Damage to oil infrastructure in that conflict and the Russia-Ukraine conflict have also put upward pressure on prices.

“Oil today is down $10,” Trump said Monday while delivering his closing midterm remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington.

“It’s going to go down a lot further because we’re winning with Iran, easily winning,” he added.

Trump claimed that the decline was “the biggest drop in oil in history.”

Recent history has seen larger drops; during the COVID-19 pandemic, oil prices on one day briefly sank to about negative $38 per barrel , falling by far more than $10.

If Monday’s drop is sustained, it could be good news for prices at the pump in the days and weeks ahead, but it can also take time for changes in the price of oil to reflect in gasoline and diesel.

Voters’ discontent with these prices is expected to be a major factor in the election. As of Monday, the average U.S. gasoline price was around $4.17 per gallon, up $1.13 from the same time last year, according to AAA .

What role with the US military take at the polls?

National Guard members in at least seven states will have some form of a role around Tuesday’s highly charged midterm elections.

As Americans head to the polls, plain clothes National Guard soldiers are set to help monitor ballot boxes in seven Washington state counties, Iowa guardsmen are tasked with monitoring and defending election networks, and Colorado Guard members will be assisting with election cybersecurity.

Those are just a few examples of the military’s role before and during Nov. 3, an election that has received intense scrutiny as Democrats look to win control of the House and Senate and President Trump has asserted he would do “anything necessary” to ensure honest elections.

A majority of Americans , however, do not think troops should be used at polling sites.

A new survey released by The Democracy and Security Network at the German Marshall Fund of the United States said those pushing back at the use of troops at the polls say it damages the public’s confidence in the military as an institution.

Loren Voss, one of the researchers who conducted the survey, said that out of the 2,800 Americans polled, 59 percent said that the president should not use the federal military to monitor or administer elections.

She told The Hill there is a generalized fear around federal interference in the elections, be it by a federalized National Guard presence, or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), or FBI agents, and having members of the military help around polling stations only adds to that concern of interference .

“This is just another instance of using the National Guard for something that should be a civilian mission ,” she said on the use of the guard at ballot boxes in Washington. “That is just so fraught for the potential of people thinking that there’s something untoward going on. articles.body:
A group of Senate Democrats accused Elon Musk’s social media platform X of giving the prediction market Polymarket “preferential treatment” on its timeline.

In a letter to X leadership Friday, Democratic Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Adam Schiff (Calif.) and Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) sent screenshots appearing to show that X does not give users the option to report Polymarket ads.

They paired the screenshots with ads for other companies — including prediction market competitor Kalshi and Musk’s Starlink product — which give users the option to “report” the advertisements.

The lawmakers questioned whether Musk was giving Polymarket “preferential treatment” since President Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., serves on the advisory board for Polymarket. Musk was a top ally of the president at the beginning of his second term, and the two have since reconciled ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, became one of the biggest financial backers of Polymarket in September. He also advises Kalshi and has a financial stake in the company.

“This seemingly preferential treatment calls into question whether X is attempting to provide an undue competitive advantage to Polymarket and – by extension – the President and his family,” the four Democratic senators wrote in the letter, which was first reported by Semafor .

The lawmakers asked Rob DeCampos, X’s chief compliance officer and head of payments compliance, whether X allows advertisers to purchase ads that cannot be reported through X’s timeline and if Polymarket’s leadership or representatives approached the social media platform about running ads with a limited “report” function.

They also asked whether the president, Trump Jr. or representatives of the Trump family approached X about running these ads.

The lawmakers referenced the 6th and 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decisions earlier this year that ruled states can regulate prediction market platforms like gambling and sportsbook.

The two rulings broke from the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals’ April decision, which allowed Kalshi to operate in New Jersey as the company’s appeal process proceeds. The court ruled Kalshi is likely to succeed in its argument that federal law preempts New Jersey’s regulation.

The contradicting rulings are teeing up a fight in the Supreme Court.

The lawmakers asked DeCampos how X “plans to ensure prediction market ads featuring sports are banned from the platform in states” following the rulings. They gave DeCampos until Nov. 30 to respond.

Polymarket, X and the Trump Organization did not immediately respond to request for comment.

articles.title: US military strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island day before midterms
articles.summary: The U.S. military struck radar detectors and missile launchers on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, a day before the U.S. midterm elections as mediators continue to push the two sides to reach a peace deal. The Monday attack is a continuation of strikes against Iran and was defensive in nature, a U.S. official told NewsNation,…
articles.body:
The U.S. military struck radar detectors and missile launchers on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, a day before the U.S. midterm elections as mediators continue to push the two sides to reach a peace deal.

The Monday attack is a continuation of strikes against Iran and was defensive in nature, a U.S. official told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

“This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets,” the official said.

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Qeshm is located in the Strait of Hormuz and is the biggest island in the Persian Gulf. The U.S. military has previously targeted the island that is a home to a naval base and an underground missile site.

The strikes, which were first reported by The Wall Street Journal, come as President Trump has said the Iran conflict would end soon after midterms.

The president has signaled that launching major combat operations is on the table after November, but Iranian officials have said it is up to the Trump administration to determine to what comes next.

“The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran’s demands are reasonable and logical,” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters on Monday.

Qatar, with the backing of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, is leading the effort to return Iran and the U.S. to the negotiating table.

Centcom has prepared multiple Iran strike options — including targeting Iranian infrastructure and military sites — that could be employed if there is authorization from the White House, The Hill previously reported .

“We had a war with Iran. We won,” the president told reporters on Monday. “I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

articles.title: Inside AI giants’ Election Day ‘war rooms’
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence firms are on high alert for Election Day, taking a page out of social media firms’ playbook to manage the flurry of information expected online in the coming days. After a dramatic few months for the AI industry, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are under pressure to ensure their products are feeding out…
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence firms are on high alert for Election Day, taking a page out of social media firms’ playbook to manage the flurry of information expected online in the coming days.

After a dramatic few months for the AI industry, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are under pressure to ensure their products are feeding out accurate information to voters.

And in the face of old and new cybersecurity threats, firms say they are also more closely watching for election interference attempts carried out with AI.

Here’s everything you need to know about how AI firms are preparing for Tuesday’s chaos, including “war rooms.”

In the two years since the last election, talk around AI and the technology’s benefits and risks to society skyrocketed in Washington and on the campaign trail. From policy debates to industry campaign spending to AI-generated ads, AI played a bigger role this midterm cycle than ever before on multiple fronts.

Research indicates voters are increasingly turning to AI chatbots or AI-generated search results when looking for election information, and they could be trusting these answers.

Like the launch of social media in the 2000s, the use of AI is raising questions over how technology influences the way voters stay informed and whether the public can trust everything they read from an AI chatbot or search result.

Lawmakers, many of whom are running for reelection, have called on AI firms and social media companies to ensure platforms’ accuracy.

In a letter to tech CEOs last month, Sens. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Reps. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) and Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) wrote, “You are aware of the great responsibility that your companies hold in America’s elections.”

“Your platforms play a significant and important role in sharing, disseminating and in some cases generating information about those elections,” the lawmakers said.

Four of the country’s largest AI firms spoke publicly in recent months on how they plan to handle the influx of information and changes in real time.

AI’s accuracy has drastically improved over the past few years, but skepticism still remains about its error rates. A study from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue in September found nearly a third of AI chatbots’ replies to election questions were incomplete, outdated or inaccurate.

The AI labs say they are focused on distributing accurate information, rather than trying to persuade a voter on their ballot decisions amid speculation on model bias.

“People should be able to access reliable information, understand the origin of AI-generated media that they might encounter off-platform and to explore kind of political questions without being steered in one particular direction by the model,” Josh Lawson, OpenAI’s head of civic and strategic risk, told reporters last month.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are partnering with Democracy Works, which compiles information on registration, deadlines, voting locations and updates throughout the election process.

This information is used to form ChatGPT’s responses and provides links to official election resources for voters, OpenAI said. The company is also partnering with The Associated Press for real-time voting results.

For election queries to Anthropic’s models, the company features a banner linking to TurboVote, Democracy Works’s nonprofit and nonpartisan resource for voter guidance.

Lawson said AI’s search function has “significantly improved” to provide more up-to-date information since 2024.

“Whenever you’re asking a question, if it’s about politics or any type of civic area, the model is almost always going to go search first,” Lawson said. “It’s not trying to answer you based on its baseline training … it is using what it understands about the world to then say, ‘Hey, this is what it seems like this person is really interested in understanding, and let’s go out and pull in sources of information that could be helpful to that person.’”

While Meta now offers AI models, this issue is nothing new for the Facebook and Instagram parent company. It reactivated its Elections Operations Center last week, which started in 2018 to quickly respond to threats of misinformation, fake accounts or harmful content leading up to and after an election. A “restriction” period also began last week, during which new political and social issue ads are prohibited given the limited time to verify new claims.

When voters ask Meta AI or Meta’s Muse model about elections, the models are supposed to give local information and direct to “authoritative government sources,” according to the company.

Google, which runs one of the most popular search engines along with AI models, also partnered with Democracy Works and the AP.

The company came under fire last week after its chatbot did not directly say who won the 2020 election, while responding normally to other election years. Google later said there was a “technical gap” with 2020 election queries, which was fixed.

“Our systems verify election responses using news articles or AP data for recent elections and historic records for older ones. 2020 was caught in between. The same was true for 2022 Senate races, which we also fixed,” the company said last Friday.

As AI advances at a rapid pace, the industry faced mounting scrutiny this year for how bad actors could utilize the technology to more easily hack into sensitive systems or infrastructure, create misleading imagery or language and eventually build powerful weapons.

Rather than tampering with a voting machine, cybersecurity experts say bad actors, including foreign influence operators, are more focused on confusing and misleading voters.

A report released earlier this year by cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found efforts to phish, impersonate and spread misinformation will be amplified by AI, giving malicious actors cheaper, broader and faster deception methods.

Taking a page out of Meta’s playbook, OpenAI and Anthropic are hosting their own “election war rooms” for the first time to monitor whether their tools are being used by bad actors.

According to OpenAI, its Election Operations Center is made up of hundreds of OpenAI employees, including the company’s top investigators and specialist teams. They will be managing “rapid response” for reviewing flagged abuse and enforcing policies or suspending and terminating accounts when needed.

Misuse will be the primary focus for OpenAI, though teams will also be managing product functionality and external requests. Politico first reported on OpenAI’s operations center.

“We’ve put considerable effort in ensuring we help users get reliable voting information, combat misuse of our tools, and support election defenders,” Lawson said in a statement shared Monday, adding the center “builds on that years-long work, bringing our teams together to respond quickly to emerging issues and enforce our policies as people head to the polls.”

Anthropic also has a dedicated war room to readily respond to technical and misuse incidents, including the use of Claude, the company confirmed to The Hill. The company defines “misuse” as using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, such as by impersonating election officials or spreading misinformation. Semafor first reported Anthropic’s election war room.

Both AI firms continuously monitor the use of their models to mislead voters or sow chaos or confusion during the electoral process.

In a threat report last month, OpenAI revealed it banned several accounts associated with propaganda operations in Iran and Russia.

Aside from text posts containing misinformation, concerns have been raised for years over the potential for deepfakes or other AI-generated audio or images impersonating officials and misleading voters.

OpenAI launched a tool for users to upload images to check whether they were made by ChatGPT. Google also offers a similar tool.

The ChatGPT maker also introduced an “image stylization” or “cartoonification” feature to avoid users requesting ultrarealistic images for election-related content. With this tool, an OpenAI model will make a cartoon-looking image that voters will easily be able to identify as fake.

Asked what types of prompts ChatGPT may “cartoonify,” Lawson pointed to images depicting long lines at polls, natural disasters and other tactics bad actors have used to mislead voters.

articles.title: Trump mulls Iran strikes after midterms, as mediators push for peace deal
articles.summary: Mediators are pushing the U.S. and Iran to reach a deal to end the war in the Middle East as President Trump mulls military strikes as early as this week. Trump has predicted the war will quickly draw to a conclusion after the midterms on Tuesday, though he’s been ambiguous about how that will happen.…
articles.body:
Mediators are pushing the U.S. and Iran to reach a deal to end the war in the Middle East as President Trump mulls military strikes as early as this week.

Trump has predicted the war will quickly draw to a conclusion after the midterms on Tuesday, though he’s been ambiguous about how that will happen. Iranian officials argued it is up to Washington to determine what comes next in the region.

“The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran’s demands are reasonable and logical,” Esmail Baghaei, a spokesperson for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, told reporters on Monday in Iran.

Qatar is leading the push for both sides to return to the negotiating table, with the backing of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey. Vice President Vance also sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei last week in an effort to revive peace talks, The Wall Street Journal reported.

However, regional experts say Trump appears to be leaning toward military escalation in the short term.

“That seems to be where Trump is headed,” Eric Brewer, deputy vice president for the nuclear materials security program at the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI), said in an interview with The Hill on Monday.

“I do think he also realizes that at the end of the day, you’re going to need some type of an agreement to end the war,” Brewer said.

Jonathan Ruhe, a fellow for American strategy at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, said all signs are pointing to a resumption of the conflict and that the president seems to think there is a “short war” option to achieve a “decisive” result.

“Trump’s most effective strategy against the Iranians is this longer-term and more patient but painful economic warfare strategy with the blockade and the aggressive sanctions,” Ruhe said in an interview.

Trump’s cycle of aggression and diplomacy toward Iran over the past eight months has not extracted any significant concessions from the Middle Eastern country.

U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, has drawn up multiple Iran strike options — including targeting Iranian infrastructure and military sites — that could be employed if there is authorization from the White House, The Hill previously reported .

Some senators were briefed in late September on the potential U.S. military strike plans. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, slammed Centcom’s plan as “insane” and said it would lead to “devastating escalation.”

“The plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests,” Murphy said last week during an appearance at the Middle East Institute.

Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of Centcom, provided the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense with a classified briefing about Iran on Sept. 29, a source familiar with the briefing told The Hill.

Iran has warned publicly and privately that its retaliation in case of renewed U.S. strikes would not be constrained to the region, putting America-linked targets across Europe on notice.

America’s allies in the Middle East and Europe are anxious to avoid another barrage of Tehran’s one-way attack drones and missiles.

Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz , through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil transits daily, on several conditions, including lifting U.S. sanctions and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. Tehran sent a delegation to Doha to meet with Qatari mediators this week.

“If Iran’s legitimate demands are accepted and implemented, it would be possible to put the entire plan into operation within two days, restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and initiate the negotiation process,” Baghaei told reporters in Iran.

“⁠The realization of this depends entirely on Washington’s will and decision,” Baghaei said.

United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told a diplomatic conference in Bahrain on Sunday that the UAE and Gulf countries are hoping for a diplomatic breakthrough.

“From the perspective of the UAE and I would also say Gulf countries, we don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region. We want to see a diplomatic and political resolution of this protracted crisis,” he said at the Manama Dialogue on Sunday.

Trump said Monday that he is in no hurry to decide whether the U.S. should return to striking Iran.

“One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it,” the president said in an interview with Axios.

Iran’s conditions are unlikely to be accepted by the Trump administration, which has demanded concessions on Iran’s nuclear program as a condition for any economic relief.

Regional experts said the U.S. military’s potential short-term strike campaign would not likely shift the negotiating dynamics.

They said despite the U.S. and Israeli military damage, which dates back to Operation Midnight Hammer, Iran has not changed its position, and “ hitting them hard again” is not going to reach a different outcome this time around.

“Iran thinks that they’ve come out of this war with more leverage, not less, because of their ability to threaten Hormuz, because they still have a lot of missile and drone capabilities, and because fundamentally they’re, you know, they still have the ultimate option of trying to go for a nuclear weapon, even though a lot of their infrastructure has been degraded,” Ruhe said.

Brewer, of NTI, said the U.S. military could strike Pickaxe Mountain, shutting down some entrances, but airstrikes can’t destroy the facility.

“There’s not a lot to be gained from a counterproliferation standpoint militarily,” Brewer said.

“Trying to convince yourself that you can strike some energy and other civilian targets within Iran, and then that Iran is going to capitulate to U.S. terms and abandon the nuclear program, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and basically not try to assert any control over that waterway, I think is pretty unlikely,” he said.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections, Axios reported .

Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, has warned against the prime minister taking any offensive military action during the next few weeks, as political parties negotiate Israel’s next government.

“Until the government is formed, I will back military moves only if there are direct and immediate threats against Israel that cannot wait until the government’s swearing-in,” Eisenkot wrote in a statement on the social platform X on Saturday.

Eisenkot earlier warned the security establishment and civil service to resist any political pressure to take action that is not in the interests of the country and its citizens.

“Stand firm against any attempt to pressure you. You have my full backing,” he said in remarks on election night.

“And Netanyahu — do not dare use Israel’s security for your own political ends,” he added.
