articles.title: OpenAI hires former Army secretary as adviser
articles.summary: OpenAI has hired former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to serve as a senior counselor for national security modernization, the company announced Monday. The ChatGPT maker said Driscoll, who stepped down from his previous role in early September, will advise the AI firm on how the technology can be used to boost national and cybersecurity. His…
articles.body:
OpenAI has hired former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to serve as a senior counselor for national security modernization, the company announced Monday.

The ChatGPT maker said Driscoll, who stepped down from his previous role in early September, will advise the AI firm on how the technology can be used to boost national and cybersecurity.

His role will focus particularly on working with U.S. allies, including working to “advance practical modernization initiatives” and helping OpenAI teams to “understand the operational needs of global national security institutions.”

“The people who serve deserve the very best tools we can put in their hands,” Driscoll said in a statement. “National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years.”

“This technology will help them keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster,” he continued. “I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.”

Driscoll resigned as Army secretary earlier this year following a lengthy turf war with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

After President Trump tapped Driscoll last year to negotiate with Ukrainian officials in an effort to end the Russia-Ukraine war, tensions flared between the two Pentagon leaders. Hegseth later fired several senior Army officials, including those close to Driscoll.

While serving as Army secretary, Driscoll had pushed to update the branch’s equipment and learn from Ukraine on how to modernize warfare capabilities using commercial technology.

articles.title: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm elections on November 3rd will determine the makeup of Congress, and how lawmakers approach issues of AI safety, data centers, and more.
articles.body: The 2026 midterm elections will determine the scope of President Donald Trump’s power in his final two years in office, and signal what voters care about going into the 2028 presidential election. While this year’s races are expected to be most broadly defined by affordability issues, there’s several topics impacting the tech industry that appear to be on voters’ minds. Among them are concerns about data centers, and whether voters will have to bear the burden of higher energy costs, AI safety, and the rapid expansion of surveillance technology through Flock. There’s also the question of how to tax billionaires’ wealth in California, a topic that has driven heavy tech spending and creative stock class structures meant to keep tech executives from fleeing the state should a ballot measure pass. The next Congress is likely to continue grappling with how to regulate AI, and stem the data center backlash, among other issues. How that conversation shapes up, and which tech CEOs are hauled to testify on Capitol Hill, will be shaped by the outcome of November 3rd.

articles.title: New York City's Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The mayor's comments come after the entertainment giant's data breach last year, which exposed James Dolan's surveillance.
articles.body:
Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani has criticized the owner of Madison Square Garden, one of the city’s largest entertainment venues, arguing that the company’s surveillance technology should not be allowed.

Mamdani told Wired in an interview on Tuesday that surveillance technologies are “indicative of much that is wrong in our country today.” He added that City Council member Shahana Hanif introduced two pieces of local legislation aimed at banning the collection of biometric data , such as using facial recognition, in public places across the city. Mamdani said that the draft legislation is “an important response to this kind of an issue.”

The comments come after a stream of reporting from Wired detailing how Madison Square Garden’s owner James Dolan relies on surveillance cameras and face-scanning technology to track people across and outside of its venues.

In one report , Wired revealed that Dolan’s company keeps a database that, among other things, marks some visitors, including celebrity performers, as “LGBTQIA,” for reasons that are unclear. Dolan subsequently sued Wired over its reporting.

In 2021, MSG made headlines after a woman was banned from Radio City, another Dolan-owned venue, after being recognized by facial recognition systems as an attorney at a law firm who was suing Dolan’s company but was not involved in the litigation.

When reached by TechCrunch, Madison Square Garden spokesperson Mikyl Cordova said: “Wired’s reporting is inaccurate and false. MSG is pursuing legal remedies,” without providing evidence for its claim.

Since 2021, New York City has required businesses to disclose when they are collecting biometric data from visitors.
